Why a transformer winding produces the voltage it does

Faraday says a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage across it: e = N · dΦ/dt. Everything a transformer does follows from that one sentence.

For a sinusoidal flux the arithmetic closes. The peak rate of change is 2πf·Φmax, and the RMS value of a sine is that divided by √2, so E = (2π/√2) · f · N · Φmax — the 4.44 every textbook prints. It is not a fudge factor; it is 2π/√2 written out.

Read the equation the other way and it explains a fault. Flux is what the voltage and frequency fix, not something the designer chooses freely: run a 50 Hz transformer at 400 V on 60 Hz and the flux falls, which is harmless. Run a 60 Hz transformer at its rated voltage on 50 Hz and the flux rises by a fifth, the core saturates, and the magnetising current goes with it.
The flux is sinusoidal. A square-wave or distorted supply changes the constant, and 4.44 is no longer the right number.
Every turn links the same flux. Leakage means the outer turns see less, which is what makes a real winding produce slightly less than this.
The core is not saturated. Past the knee the flux stops following the current and this equation stops describing the machine.
Reluctance, flux and flux density — Ohm\'s law with different names

A magnetic circuit is the same arithmetic as an electric one with the labels changed. Magnetomotive force F = N·I drives flux Φ through a reluctance ℛ, exactly as voltage drives current through resistance: Φ = F / ℛ.

Reluctance depends on the path the same way resistance does — ℛ = l / (μ₀·μr·A) — and the analogy carries far enough to be genuinely useful: reluctances in series add, a high-permeability core is a low-reluctance path that gathers flux the way a copper conductor gathers current, and an air gap is an enormous resistor in the middle of it.

That last point is where the analogy earns its keep. Steel has a relative permeability in the thousands and air has one. A millimetre of gap in a 300 mm path can dominate the whole circuit, which is why motor designers count air gaps in tenths of a millimetre.
Permeability is taken as constant. Real steel saturates, and above about 1.5 T the relative permeability collapses and this calculation overstates the flux badly.
The flux is spread evenly over the cross-section and stays inside the core. Fringing at corners and leakage into the air are not counted.
No air gap. One gap of a fraction of a millimetre can outweigh the whole steel path, so a gapped core has to be worked as reluctances in series.

What a turns ratio does to voltage, current and impedance

An ideal transformer conserves power. Whatever goes in comes out, so if the voltage rises the current must fall in the same proportion: Up/Us = Np/Ns = Is/Ip.

Impedance is the part that surprises people. A load on the secondary looks, from the primary, like that load multiplied by the square of the turns ratio — because the voltage transforms one way and the current the other, and impedance is their quotient. A 4 Ω speaker behind a 10:1 transformer presents 400 Ω to the amplifier, which is the entire reason matching transformers exist.

The ratio is fixed by the windings and nothing else. A transformer cannot regulate: what a tap changer does is switch between windings, not adjust one.
Lossless and perfectly coupled. A real transformer has winding resistance and leakage reactance, so the secondary voltage falls as it is loaded — the regulation this calculation shows as zero.
No magnetising current. A real primary draws some even with the secondary open, which is what makes a no-load reading look wrong against this.
An impedance expressed against the system it sits in

An impedance in ohms means nothing until you say which side of which transformer it was measured on. Five ohms is a short circuit at 400 V and a rounding error at 400 kV.

Per-unit fixes that by dividing every quantity by a base of the same kind. Choose a base power and a base voltage; the base impedance follows as U²/S, and every impedance in the network becomes a dimensionless number. The point is what happens at a transformer: per-unit values pass straight through it. The same figure describes the same component from either side, which is what makes a network with four voltage levels solvable by hand.

It is also why manufacturers print transformer impedance as a percentage. Per cent is per-unit multiplied by a hundred, on the transformer's own rating as the base.

Three-phase quantities throughout: S is the three-phase power and U the line-to-line voltage. Mixing a single-phase base into the same calculation introduces a factor of three that is very hard to find later.
One base for the whole network. Manufacturer impedances come on the equipment\'s own rating and must be converted before they can be added to anything.

Which limit binds depends on how the cables lie. Four 20 mm cables across a 100 mm tray take 80 % of its width but only 21 % of its cross-section — an area percentage alone would call that tray four fifths empty when nothing more can be laid in it.

Power cables are normally laid in a single layer so each can shed heat to the air. Stacking them is what forces the grouping derating up, and a tray that passes on area can still be a thermal problem.

Geometry is not the usual failure. A tray is rated in kg per metre of span, and a full tray of copper reaches that long before it looks full. Total the cable weights and check them against the tray\'s rated load and support spacing.

Two currents come out because two decisions need them, and using one where the other belongs is the mistake this calculator exists to prevent. The maximum (c = 1.05, conductor cold) is the most a device may have to interrupt. The minimum (c = 0.95, conductor at its rated temperature) is a fault at the end of a fully loaded cable — the least current the device will ever see, and the figure that proves it trips.

Copper gains about 20 % resistance between 20 °C and its 70 °C PVC rating, and about 27 % at the 90 °C XLPE rating. On a long run that alone separates the two currents by more than the voltage factors do.

A line–neutral fault returns through the neutral, so both conductors are in the loop and the current is roughly half the three-phase figure. A reduced neutral makes it lower still. This is the fault that fails to trip, not the three-phase one.

Supply and cable impedances are added as magnitudes, which is what loop impedance testers and IEC 60364 practice do. Their angles differ — a transformer-fed supply is mostly reactive, an LV cable mostly resistive — so the sum slightly overstates the loop and the current comes out a little low. That is the safe direction for verifying disconnection. Close to the origin, where breaking capacity is being selected, use a full IEC 60909 study.

A fault current on its own proves nothing. Compare the minimum against the current that operates the device in the required time, and check that the protective conductor survives the let-through energy. Both are in the Earth Fault Loop calculator.

A circuit needs both verdicts. Disconnection asks whether enough current flows to operate the device. Withstand asks whether the protective conductor survives the energy that flows while it does. A cable can pass the first and fail the second, which is how an installation clears its fault and melts its earth in the same instant.

The device\'s curve decides as much as the cable does. A Type C needs ten times its rating to trip where a Type B needs five, so it needs half the loop impedance. The same cable, the same length, a different breaker — and a circuit that passed now fails.

R₁ and R₂ are taken at the insulation\'s rated temperature, not at 20 °C. A fault is most likely on a warm cable, and a warm cable has the highest resistance and therefore the lowest fault current. Computing them cold flatters the answer in exactly the direction that matters.

The everyday failure is length. A run can be correct on current-carrying capacity and correct on voltage drop and still leave the device unable to see a fault at its far end. That is why this check is separate from cable sizing rather than folded into it.

A residual current device is judged differently: it responds to the imbalance between line and neutral, not to the size of the fault current, so the criterion is touch voltage — Zs × IΔn ≤ 50 V. A 30 mA device tolerates about 1667 Ω, which is why a TT installation works at all.

IEC 60364-5-54 permits two routes for the protective conductor: the calculation shown here, or the table rule (S ≤ 16 → S, 16–35 → 16, above 35 → S/2). Both are reported. The table is quicker and usually the larger conductor; either satisfies the standard.

The k values are for a protective conductor incorporated in a cable or bunched with cables, from IEC 60364-5-54 Table 54.3. A conductor run separately is allowed a higher final temperature and a larger k; using these for that case is safe but not the right table.
Ze and the finished Zs should both be measured, not only calculated. A computed loop assumes every connection is sound; the measurement is what proves it.

An MCB trips with a normal load
Establish whether it trips instantly or after a while. Instant is magnetic and means current; delayed is thermal and means heat.
Trips instantly on switch-on: inrush. A transformer, a motor or a bank of LED drivers wants a Type C or D, not a Type B.
Trips after several minutes: thermal. The load is genuinely near the rating, or the breaker is hot.
A hot consumer unit. Breakers derate with temperature, and a board full of them in a warm cupboard runs well above room ambient.
Neighbouring circuits loaded at the same time. Heat from the breakers either side is enough to shift the thermal characteristic.
Harmonic current. An RMS-reading clamp shows more than a mean-reading one, and the breaker responds to the real heating.
A genuine intermittent short — a screw through a cable, a chafed strand — which shows as an instant trip that will not reset.
Errors that pass inspection, work for years, and then do not.
Why these are the dangerous ones
Every item here produces an installation that works. That is exactly the problem: nothing complains, the job is signed off, and the defect waits for the one condition that turns it into an incident.
If you find one of these on an existing installation, assume it is not the only one. They cluster: whoever made this decision made the others too.
Load a realistic job and see it worked through.
Try the English spelling, or part of the word.
The part of the supplied power that does real work — turns a shaft, makes heat, gives light. It is what an energy meter bills.

A check that a conductor survives a fault long enough for the protective device to clear it, using S ≥ √(I²t)/k from IEC 60364-5-54. It assumes none of the heat escapes during the fault, which is why it is called adiabatic.

The air temperature around a cable or a device, before it heats anything itself. Capacity tables assume 30 °C in air; hotter surroundings leave a conductor less room to shed its own heat, so its rating falls.

The current a conductor can carry continuously without its insulation exceeding its rated temperature. It is a property of the installation, not just the cable: the same conductor buried, in a tray or in insulation has three different figures.
Voltage times current, without regard to how much of it does work. Cables and transformers are sized on this, because they carry the whole current whether it is useful or not.

A fault where current jumps a gap instead of flowing through metal, at a damaged terminal or a broken strand. The current can stay below what an overcurrent device would trip on while the arc itself is hot enough to start a fire.

A steel wire or tape layer under a cable\'s outer sheath, there to take mechanical damage. It also gives the cable an earthed metallic path, which is why armoured cable is common where a separate protective conductor would be awkward.
The standard protective measure of IEC 60364-4-41: an earth fault must raise enough current to operate the protective device within a stated time, so a dangerous touch voltage cannot persist.
American Wire Gauge, the North American conductor size scale. The numbers run backwards — larger gauge means thinner wire — and each step of three roughly halves the area.
An upstream device that assists a downstream one whose breaking capacity is lower than the fault current at its terminals. The pair is only valid in combinations the manufacturer has tested.
Protection against touching a part that is live in normal service — insulation, enclosures, barriers. It is the layer that has to fail before fault protection is called on.
The largest fault current a device can interrupt and still be safe afterwards. It is selected against the maximum prospective short-circuit current at the point of installation, not against the load.
A rigid conductor, usually a copper or aluminium bar, that distributes current to several outgoing circuits inside a board.
Discharge or charge current expressed as a multiple of a battery\'s rated capacity. A 100 Ah bank at 0,5 C is being worked at 50 A.
Deliberately letting an upstream breaker help clear a fault that exceeds a downstream one\'s own breaking capacity. It saves cost but gives up selectivity, since both devices open.
A switching device that carries current normally and interrupts it automatically under overload or short circuit. Unlike a fuse it is reset rather than replaced.
The shortest distance through air between two conductive parts. Together with creepage distance it decides how close live parts may sit at a given voltage.
The metal part of a cable that carries current — copper or aluminium in practice. Everything else in the cable exists to insulate it, protect it or hold it together.
An electrically operated switch built to make and break load current repeatedly, and to drop out when its coil loses supply. That last property is what a relay is not designed for.
A dead test measuring the resistance of protective and line conductors end to end, to prove they are unbroken and correctly connected. The reading is compared against the calculated R1+R2.

A multiplier applied to a tabulated current capacity to account for conditions worse than the table assumed — hot air, bunched circuits, soil thermal resistivity. Factors multiply together, so two mild ones can bite harder than either alone.

The ratio of active power to apparent power. At cos φ = 0,8 a cable carries a quarter more current than the useful power alone would suggest, and that extra current is what gets billed as reactive energy.
The shortest path along an insulating surface between two conductive parts. Dirt and damp make a surface conduct long before air breaks down, so this is usually the larger requirement.

The conductor\'s area in mm², the number that names a cable in IEC countries. It sets both resistance and current capacity, but not in the same proportion — doubling the area halves resistance while capacity rises by rather less.

An instrument transformer that produces a small secondary current proportional to a large primary one, for metering and protection. Its secondary must never be left open-circuit while primary current flows — the voltage that appears is dangerous.
Maximum demand divided by total connected load. It recognises that not everything installed runs at once, and it is regional and regulation-specific rather than universal.
The share of a battery\'s capacity actually used before recharging. Lead-acid life falls sharply past about 50 %; lithium tolerates 80–90 %.

Reducing a component\'s usable rating because the conditions are worse than the ones it was rated in. For cables it is the ambient and grouping factors; for a device it may be temperature inside an enclosure.
How long a protective device may take to clear an earth fault. IEC 60364-4-41 requires 0,4 s for final circuits up to 32 A on a TN system and 5 s for distribution circuits.
The enclosure where an incoming supply is split into outgoing circuits, each with its own protective device.
An allowance for loads that do not peak together, used to size a supply for less than the arithmetic sum of its circuits. Like demand factor it is set by local practice, not by physics.
The metal in contact with soil that gives an installation its connection to earth — a rod, plate, tape or the building\'s foundation steel. Its resistance depends on soil far more than on the metal.

The total impedance of the path a fault current takes from the transformer, out along the line conductor, through the fault, and back along the protective conductor. It decides how much current flows, and therefore whether the device operates.
Connecting conductive parts to the general mass of earth so that a fault produces a current large enough to be detected, and so that exposed metal cannot sit at a dangerous voltage.
Output power divided by input power. The difference is loss, and it is why a 5,5 kW motor draws more than 5,5 kW from the supply.
Joining metalwork together so that no dangerous voltage can appear between two things a person might touch at once. It works by removing the difference rather than by removing the fault.
Metal belonging to equipment that is not live in normal service but could become live under a fault — a motor frame, a metal enclosure. These are what the protective conductor connects.
The part of the earth fault loop that lies outside the installation, from the origin back through the supply network. Measured at the origin or taken from the distributor\'s declared maximum.
Metal that is not part of the electrical installation but can bring a potential into it — water pipes, structural steel, gas pipes. Bonded, not earthed as a protective conductor.
The current that flows when insulation fails and a live conductor reaches earth or another conductor. Its size decides both whether the protection operates and how much damage is done before it does.
Protection against electric shock from a part that has become live because of a fault. Usually delivered by automatic disconnection of supply.
How far an assembly separates its busbars, functional units and terminals from one another, graded Form 1 to Form 4 in IEC 61439. Higher forms let one circuit be worked on while others stay live.
How many times per second an alternating supply completes a cycle. 50 Hz across most of the world, 60 Hz in North America and parts of Asia; it changes reactance, motor speed and transformer sizing.
An earth connection made so equipment works properly — screening, reference potential for electronics — rather than for safety. It does not substitute for a protective earth.
A protective device that clears a fault by melting. Its speed rises steeply with current, so it can be very fast on a short circuit while tolerating a brief overload.
A general-purpose fuse link that protects against both overload and short circuit. An aM link protects only against short circuit and must be paired with a separate overload device.

The derating applied when circuits are bunched together, because each one\'s heat makes it harder for its neighbours to cool. Nine circuits in a bundle can lose nearly half the rating of one on its own.

A current or voltage component at a whole multiple of the supply frequency, drawn by electronic loads. The third and its multiples add up in the neutral instead of cancelling, so a neutral can carry more than any line.
A two-digit rating from IEC 62262 for how much mechanical impact an enclosure withstands, from IK00 (unprotected) to IK10 (20 joules).
Luminous flux arriving per square metre of a surface. It is what a light meter reads and what a lighting design is specified in — an office typically 500 lx.
The total opposition an AC circuit presents to current: resistance and reactance combined. Unlike resistance it depends on frequency.

The percentage of rated primary voltage needed to drive rated current through a transformer with its secondary short-circuited. It is on the nameplate, and it sets the fault current the transformer can deliver.
Touching metal that has become live through a fault, rather than a conductor that is live by design. The older name for what the standards now cover as fault protection.

The opposition an inductance presents to alternating current, rising with frequency. In LV cable it is small next to resistance until the conductor gets large, at which point neglecting it understates voltage drop.
The opposition a capacitance presents to alternating current, falling as frequency rises. It is what a correction capacitor uses to supply reactive power.
The brief, large current a transformer, motor or capacitive load draws at the instant it is switched on. It is what a Type C or D breaker exists to tolerate.
The magnetic part of a breaker\'s operation, which opens it within milliseconds once current exceeds a multiple of its rating — 5× for Type B, 10× for C, 20× for D.
Resistance measured between conductors, and between conductors and earth, with a DC test voltage. IEC 60364-6 wants at least 1,0 MΩ on a 230/400 V circuit tested at 500 V.
A mechanical or electrical arrangement that makes an unsafe combination impossible — two contactors that can never close together, a door that cannot open while a circuit is live.
Two digits from IEC 60529: the first is protection against solids and contact, the second against water. IP54 is dust-protected and splash-proof.
Cutting an installation off from every source of supply, with a visible or positively indicated gap, so it can be worked on safely. Switching off a load is not isolation.

An earthing arrangement with no direct connection between supply and earth, or one through a high impedance. A first earth fault does not produce enough current to trip, which is why the system keeps running and why insulation monitoring is mandatory.
The energy a protective device allows past before it clears a fault, in A²s. The cable\'s withstand must exceed it — that is the adiabatic check, written the other way round.
A conductor that carries current from the source to the load and is live in normal service. Marked L1, L2, L3 on a three-phase system; brown, black and grey under IEC 60446.
A conductor or conductive part intended to be energised in normal use, including the neutral. The neutral counts, which is why it is switched and isolated like any other live conductor.
Average load over a period divided by the peak load in that period. It describes how evenly a supply is used, and it is a tariff and sizing input rather than a safety one.
Low smoke zero halogen cable compound. It burns without producing the dense acidic smoke that PVC does, which matters in tunnels, ships and public buildings where people evacuate through the smoke.
The total light a source emits, in lumens. A lamp is sold by this figure; how much of it reaches the working plane depends on the luminaire, the room and its surfaces.
Miniature circuit breaker: the DIN-rail device protecting final circuits, made to IEC 60898. Its trip curve — B, C or D — is what decides whether an earth fault disconnects fast enough.
Moulded case circuit breaker, made to IEC 60947-2 for larger currents than an MCB. Its trip settings are usually adjustable, which is what makes selectivity achievable in a distribution board.

The plate on a machine stating the conditions it was designed and tested for. Every rating on it is conditional — a motor\'s current is at its rated voltage, frequency and duty, not at whatever it happens to see.

The conductor connected to the star point that carries the unbalance of a three-phase system back to source. It is a live conductor, and on a harmonic-rich supply it can carry more current than any line.

The power a transformer consumes just by being energised — iron loss in the core. It runs 24 hours a day whether or not anything is connected, which is why it dominates the lifetime cost of a lightly loaded transformer.
Any current above the rated value, whether from an overload or a short circuit. The two need different protection responses, which is why devices have both a thermal and a magnetic element.
Excess current in a circuit that is otherwise healthy — too much load, not a fault. It is a thermal problem, so protection may take minutes rather than milliseconds.

A single conductor doing the job of both neutral and protective earth, as in a TN-C system. It must never be switched or broken — losing it puts full line voltage on every exposed metal part it served.
The rule that a battery gives less than its nameplate capacity when discharged faster than the rate it was rated at. A lead-acid bank rated over 20 hours delivers noticeably less over 2.
How far current lags or leads voltage in an AC circuit. Its cosine is the power factor, and its sign says whether the load is inductive or capacitive.
The order in which the three line voltages reach their peaks. Reversing it reverses a motor, which is why it is verified before a machine is first run.
A check that switches and protective devices are in the line conductor and not in the neutral. Get it wrong and a circuit stays live with its switch off.
Adding capacitors to supply reactive power locally so it is not drawn from the network. Active power is unchanged; what falls is current, and with it the load on cables and transformers.
The current that would flow into a bolted fault at a given point. Two figures matter: the maximum, which selects breaking capacity, and the minimum, which verifies the device trips at all.
The conductor that connects exposed metal to earth so a fault current has a path back to source. Green-and-yellow, and never used for anything else.
Polyvinyl chloride cable insulation, rated to a 70 °C conductor temperature. Cheap and common; it softens with heat and gives off dense acidic smoke in a fire.
The current a device is designed to carry continuously, In on its nameplate. For a protective device it is also the base that trip multiples are measured from.
The voltage equipment is designed for. IEC 60038 sets 230/400 V for LV distribution, with tolerances that a design has to work inside rather than at.
One device combining residual current protection with overcurrent protection for a single circuit. An RCCB has no overcurrent element and still needs a breaker or fuse alongside it.
A residual current circuit breaker with no overcurrent protection of its own. It detects earth leakage only, so the circuit still needs a device for overload and short circuit.

A device that compares the current going out with the current coming back and opens when the difference exceeds its rating. It responds to leakage, not to how large the fault current is — which is why it protects where an overcurrent device cannot.
Power that flows back and forth between source and load without doing net work, exchanged by inductance and capacitance. It does no work but it does occupy the cable.

The installation arrangement a capacity table is written for — clipped direct, in conduit, buried, in insulation. Choosing the wrong one is the most common way a correct-looking cable calculation ends up wrong.
An electrically operated switch for control signals rather than load current. A contactor is built to break motor current; a relay generally is not.
The vector sum of the currents in all live conductors of a circuit. In a healthy circuit it is zero; anything else is current escaping to earth.

How strongly a material resists current, independent of its shape. It rises with temperature, so a hot conductor drops more voltage than the same cable cold — about 20 % more for copper between 20 °C and 70 °C.
Root mean square: the DC value that would produce the same heating. Every AC voltage and current quoted without qualification is an RMS figure — 230 V RMS peaks at about 325 V.

Arranging protection so only the device nearest a fault opens, leaving the rest of the installation running. Achieved by current, by time, or by energy — and a manufacturer\'s table is the only proof for the last of these.
A multiplier on a motor\'s rated power saying how much continuous overload it tolerates. A 1,15 service factor is headroom for occasional excess, not a licence to run there.
The outermost layer of a cable, protecting everything inside from moisture, chemicals and abrasion. It is not insulation and must never be relied on as such.
A fault of negligible impedance between conductors, producing the largest current a circuit can deliver. It is limited only by the impedance of the supply and the cable between it and the fault.

The tendency of alternating current to crowd into the outside of a conductor, leaving the centre carrying less. It is negligible in small LV cable and is the reason very large conductors are used in parallel rather than as one.

The difference between an induction motor\'s synchronous speed and its actual speed, as a fraction. A motor with no slip produces no torque — the slip is what induces rotor current in the first place.
A device that ramps voltage up so a motor accelerates gently, cutting inrush and mechanical shock. It reduces starting torque as well, so it does not suit every load.

A device that limits transient overvoltages from lightning or switching by diverting the surge to earth. It protects against voltage spikes, not against overcurrent, and has no role in fault protection.
Starting a motor with its windings in star, then switching to delta once it is up to speed. Starting current drops to a third — and so does starting torque, which is the catch.
The collective name for the devices that switch, protect and isolate circuits, together with the assemblies housing them.

The two mechanisms in a common breaker: a bimetal that responds slowly to sustained overload, and an electromagnet that responds in milliseconds to short circuit. Overload and short circuit need different speeds, so they get different mechanisms.

An earthing arrangement where exposed metal is connected back to the source\'s earthed point by a protective conductor. The fault path is metallic, so fault current is high and overcurrent devices can clear an earth fault.
The voltage appearing between parts a person can touch simultaneously during a fault. IEC 60364-4-41 takes 50 V AC as the limit that may persist in dry conditions.
A machine that changes voltage between two windings by magnetic coupling, with no moving parts. It transfers apparent power, which is why it is rated in kVA and not in kW.
The graph of operating time against current for a protective device. Reading it is how you answer both questions that matter: will it hold the load, and will it clear the fault in time.
An earthing arrangement where the installation has its own earth electrode, separate from the supply\'s. Loop impedance is high, so an RCD rather than an overcurrent device provides fault protection.
A code such as Dyn11 giving a transformer\'s winding connections and the phase shift between them. Transformers must match on this before they can be paralleled.
An electronic drive that varies a motor\'s speed by varying supply frequency. It draws a distorted, high-frequency-rich current, which is why it needs a Type B RCD and careful cable screening.
The voltage lost along a cable because the conductor has resistance. IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G suggests keeping it within 3 % for lighting and 5 % for other circuits, measured from the origin.
A tolerance IEC 60909 applies to nominal voltage so each fault calculation errs the safe way: 1,05 for a maximum current, 0,95 for a minimum.
The current a component can carry for a stated short time without damage — a busbar\'s 1-second rating, for instance. It is a thermal and mechanical limit, not an operating rating.
Cross-linked polyethylene cable insulation, rated to a 90 °C conductor temperature. The higher rating means more current for the same section than PVC, but the cable is stiffer to install.
Why it is done that way, and what goes wrong

A non-contact voltage detector cannot prove a circuit dead

It senses the field around a conductor, so it reports what is nearby rather than what is in front of it. Screened cable, a conductor at the back of a bunch, a low battery or a gloved hand between pen and cable all give the same result as a dead circuit: nothing. Use it to find a live conductor, never to establish that one is dead — that needs a two-pole tester, proved on a known source before and after.
A disconnected conductor can read most of the supply voltage

A long run beside a live cable couples to it capacitively. A digital multimeter draws almost no current, so that coupling is enough to show a hundred volts or more on a conductor that is disconnected at both ends. The reading is real; the source behind it cannot deliver current. A two-pole tester loads the circuit and collapses the phantom, which is the whole reason it is the tool for proving dead.
Isolating a circuit does not discharge what is in it

Power-factor correction banks and the DC link inside a drive hold their charge after the supply is gone, and both store enough energy to be lethal. Discharge resistors take time and they fail silently. Wait for the time the manufacturer states, then prove it dead at the terminals — the wait is a prerequisite for the test, not a substitute for it.
The test button on an RCD proves the RCD, not the installation

It drives a current through an internal winding to check that the mechanism still releases. It says nothing about the earth path, the trip time under a real fault, or whether the device is wired the right way round. A button that works on an installation with no earth connection still works — and the installation is still lethal.
A neutral is a live conductor, not a safe one

It sits near earth potential only while the circuit is intact and reasonably balanced. Open it while load is connected and the far end rises towards line voltage; unbalance a three-phase circuit and it carries current that has to go somewhere. Treat it as live until proved otherwise, and never disconnect one on a circuit you have not isolated.
A broken PEN conductor puts line voltage on every earthed surface

In a TN-C-S supply the incoming conductor is neutral and earth in one. Lose it upstream and load current returns through the only path left — the earthing system — so exposed metalwork throughout the installation rises towards line potential while every device keeps working normally. Nothing trips, nothing looks wrong. It is the reason TN-C-S is not permitted for some installations at all.
A borrowed neutral stays live after you isolate its circuit

Where an installation has grown, a circuit\'s neutral is sometimes connected to a different circuit\'s line. Switch off the breaker you believe feeds the work and the line goes dead while the neutral keeps carrying another circuit\'s current. Common in lighting on two-way switching and in old rewires. If a supposedly dead neutral reads a voltage or sparks on disconnection, stop and find where it goes.
Choose the meter by where you are standing, not by the voltage

Measurement category rates a tester for the transient energy at a location, not for the steady voltage it will read. Nearer the origin, the impedance behind the fault is lower and the transients are larger: a socket outlet is CAT II, a distribution board CAT III, the incomer and the supply side CAT IV. A CAT II meter reading 230 V perfectly well at an intake can still fail as an arc across your hands.
A fuse is chosen for its breaking capacity as much as its rating

Two fuses of the same amperage are not interchangeable. The class sets how it behaves before it clears — gG for general circuits, aM for motors that must survive inrush — and the breaking capacity sets the fault current it can interrupt without rupturing. Fitting a higher rating to stop nuisance operation removes the protection the cable was sized around, and the cable is now the fuse.
An emergency stop is not an isolator

It is designed to bring machinery to a safe state quickly, and it can often be reset from somewhere you cannot see. It may leave control circuits, heaters or a drive\'s DC link energised, and on many machines it does. Isolation means a device intended for isolation, locked in the off position, with the key in your pocket.
Switching a device off leaves its own terminals live

Open a breaker and the load side is dead while its supply terminals stay at full voltage — that is what it is for. The same is true of an isolator, a contactor and a switched socket. To work on the device itself you have to isolate the thing feeding it, which is usually one board further back than people expect.
An unlabelled board is a hazard you leave behind for someone else

Every hour saved by not labelling is paid back with interest by whoever next has to isolate a circuit in a hurry. Guessing which breaker feeds what ends either in the wrong circuit being switched off — sometimes one that mattered — or in the right one being left on. Label as you go: the information is in your head only while you are standing there.
On a long run the volt drop limit is reached before the current rating

Ampacity is set by how hot the conductor gets, which does not care how far it goes. Volt drop accumulates with every metre. Past roughly thirty or forty metres on a final circuit the cable that carries the current comfortably is already outside the drop limit, so size on drop first and check the rating afterwards — doing it the other way round means sizing twice.
Double the length and you double the drop; double the area and you halve it

Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, so both relationships are exactly linear and both are worth having in your head. A run that drops 3 % at 25 m drops 6 % at 50 m. Going up one preferred size is not a halving though — the series steps by roughly 1.5 to 1.6 at a time, so one size buys about a third off the drop, not half.
At 230 V single phase, a kilowatt is about 4.3 A

For a resistive load — heating, filament lighting, a kettle — current is simply power over voltage. It is the fastest sanity check there is on a nameplate or a schedule of loads. For anything with a motor or a switched-mode supply, divide by the power factor as well, which for a small motor takes 4.3 A closer to 5.5 A.
At 400 V three phase, a kilowatt is about 1.44 A

The √3 in the three-phase formula is what makes the same power need less current per conductor than a single-phase supply of the same voltage. Carrying 1.44 A per kilowatt lets you size a submain in your head and catch a schedule of loads that is out by a factor rather than a percent.
A 400 V transformer gives about 1.44 A on the secondary per kVA

The same √3 arithmetic, run on apparent power instead of active: a 630 kVA unit delivers roughly 910 A at full load. Useful standing in front of a transformer with no nameplate legible, and the number the incoming device and busbar have to be rated for.
A motor started direct-on-line draws six to eight times its full load current

For the second or two it takes to reach speed. It is why the protective device has to tolerate an inrush it would otherwise treat as a fault, why a gG fuse is the wrong choice in front of a motor, and why a supply that runs the motor perfectly well can still dim the lights every time it starts.
Copper gains about 0.4 % resistance per kelvin

A conductor at its 70 °C limit has roughly 20 % more resistance than the same conductor at 20 °C, and therefore 20 % more volt drop. Calculating drop at ambient and then loading the cable to its rating is how a design that passed on paper fails on site.
Bunching circuits together costs more capacity than the ambient ever does

Six circuits in one containment lose over 40 % of their tabulated rating; the same cables would have to reach about 55 °C ambient to lose as much. Grouping is also the factor most often left out, because it is a property of the installation rather than of the cable in front of you.
The device rating has to sit between the load and the cable

Design current ≤ device rating ≤ cable capacity, in that order, with no exceptions worth learning as a beginner. Every overload argument reduces to those two inequalities: a device smaller than the load nuisance-trips, a device larger than the cable leaves the cable unprotected.
Correcting power factor cuts current, not the energy you are billed for

Capacitors return reactive current locally instead of dragging it up the supply, so cables and transformers see less current and the losses in them fall. The active energy the meter records barely moves. The saving is in released capacity and in avoiding a reactive charge, which is a different argument from a smaller electricity bill.
Light the task, not the room

Illuminance targets are written against what is being done — a workshop bench and the corridor outside it differ by a factor of five. Designing to one figure for a whole building over-lights the circulation and under-lights the work, and the lumen method gives an average across a plane, so a compliant average can still leave a dark bench under a badly placed fitting.
Diversity is an argument about behaviour, not a coefficient to apply

It says that not every load runs at once, which is true of sockets in a house and false of a machine line built to run flat out. Applying a habitual factor to a load that has no diversity is how a submain ends up undersized, and the failure appears at commissioning under real load rather than on paper.
Every dead test comes before the first live one

Continuity and insulation resistance are done on an isolated installation, and they are what tells you it is safe to energise. Running them afterwards inverts the point: the first fault they would have found has already been found by putting voltage on it. The order is the test, not a preference.
An insulation test at 500 V will destroy anything left connected

Dimmers, LED drivers, surge protection and any electronic control are not built to survive the test voltage. Disconnect them or link out the circuit, and remember that a device damaged this way often keeps working for a while — the failure arrives weeks later and nobody connects it to the test.
Loop impedance is only meaningful at the furthest point of the circuit

It rises with distance, so the reading at the board is the best case and the reading at the last socket is the one the disconnection time depends on. A circuit that passes at the board and fails at its end is a circuit that will not disconnect in time under a fault where a fault is most likely.
A reversed line and neutral leaves everything switched on the neutral

Lamps light, sockets work, and every appliance behaves normally — the fault shows up only when someone opens a switched fitting and finds the line conductor still connected to the part they are holding. It takes seconds to check and there is no symptom to notice later.
A residual current device that trips at the right current can still be too slow

Trip current and trip time are separate results. A device operating at 25 mA on a 30 mA rating has the sensitivity but might exceed 300 ms, which is what determines whether it protects a person. Record both; a pass on one is not a pass.
The protective conductor is the first thing to prove and the easiest to forget

Every other protective measure assumes it is there. A high-resistance joint in it — a painted enclosure, an overtightened terminal, a strand cut through — leaves the installation looking normal and disconnecting slowly or not at all, and no test of the line conductors reveals it.
A clamp around a whole cable reads nearly zero, and that is correct

Line and neutral currents are equal and opposite, so their fields cancel and the instrument reports the difference — which is the leakage. To measure load current, clamp one conductor. Reading a few milliamps around the whole cable is not a broken meter; it is the earth leakage, and a rising one is worth investigating.
An averaging meter under-reads distorted current badly

Meters that are not true RMS assume a sine wave and scale an average to suit it. On the current drawn by LED drivers, drives and switched-mode supplies that assumption is wrong and the reading can be tens of per cent low — precisely on the circuits whose neutral current is the thing you were worried about.

A recorded 0.35 Ω is comparable with next year\'s 0.55 Ω and shows a joint going high before it fails. A recorded \"pass\" tells the next person only that someone once thought it was fine. The value of a test schedule is almost entirely in the trend.
Null the leads, or their resistance lands in every continuity reading

A pair of leads is easily 0.1 Ω, which is a large fraction of the figure a short final circuit should show. Nulling takes a moment at the start of the day; skipping it systematically inflates every reading and turns a genuinely low resistance into a borderline one.
A circuit can pass insulation testing and still be broken

Insulation resistance proves conductors are separated from each other and from earth. It says nothing about whether a conductor is continuous. A neutral broken inside a joint gives an excellent insulation reading — infinite, in fact — because a disconnected conductor is very well insulated indeed.
Energise one circuit at a time, and know what each one should draw

Closing everything at once means an inrush that is the sum of every load and a fault that could be anywhere. Bringing circuits up one by one localises a problem to the last thing you switched, and it lets you compare the current drawn against what that circuit was designed for while there is still time to act on the difference.

Voltage, current and resistance — the relationship everything else is built on

The current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across it. Double the voltage and the current doubles; the constant of proportionality is what we call resistance.

That proportionality is less a law of nature than a description of a class of materials. Metals hold to it closely over a wide range, which is why it gets called a law at all. A filament lamp does not: its resistance climbs as the filament heats, so measuring it cold and calculating a running current gives a figure several times too high.

Everything downstream is this one relationship applied to a busier circuit — the series and parallel rules, the divider, and the whole of alternating current once resistance is generalised to impedance.
The material is ohmic: its resistance does not change with the current through it.
Temperature is constant. Copper gains roughly four parts in a thousand of resistance per kelvin, so a warm cable is not the cable you measured cold.
Direct current, or alternating current through a purely resistive load. Anything with inductance or capacitance needs impedance in place of resistance.
Three forms of the same product, and why you rarely need the one you remember

Power is the rate at which energy is converted. In a resistive circuit that is the voltage across the component multiplied by the current through it: every coulomb that crosses gives up an amount of energy set by the voltage, and the current says how many cross per second.

Substituting Ohm’s law into that product gives two more forms, and they are the useful ones. You almost never have both a voltage and a current in hand: you have a measured current and a known resistance, or a supply voltage and a resistance. The three forms all give the same watts, so use whichever matches what you already know rather than going back to find a third quantity.

The squared terms are worth noticing. Doubling the current through a fixed resistance does not double the heat — it quadruples it. That is why a slightly overloaded conductor gets hot so much faster than the overload suggests.
Direct current, or alternating current through a purely resistive load. With a phase angle in play this gives apparent power, not the power that does work.
All the energy leaves as heat. A motor or a lamp converts some of it to work or light, and its resistance is not the whole story.
One path, one current, and a supply voltage shared out in proportion

Components end to end form one path, so the same current passes through every one of them. There is nowhere for charge to go but onward.

The voltages are the opposite. Each resistance takes a share of the supply set by Ohm’s law on that same current, so the shares are in proportion to the resistances and they add back to the supply exactly. That sum is worth using as a check: measure the drops around a series circuit and they must total the supply voltage, and if they do not, something in the loop is not what you think it is.

This is why a long cable run costs voltage at the load. The conductor is a resistance in series with whatever it feeds, and it takes its share before the load sees any of it.
There is exactly one path. A single extra connection anywhere turns part of the circuit into a parallel network and the shared-current rule stops holding.
The wire between components has no resistance of its own. Over a long run it does, and that is a resistance in the series just like the others.
One current for the whole loop
One voltage, currents that add, and a total smaller than the smallest branch

Components across the same pair of nodes all see the same voltage, because they are connected to the same two points. What differs is how much current each one lets through, and those currents add up to what the supply delivers.

Working in conductances rather than resistances makes this obvious: conductance is how freely a branch passes current, and adding a branch can only add more ways through. So the combined resistance is always smaller than the smallest branch — not an average of them, which is the mistake this rule invites.

Every socket circuit in a building is this. Adding a load does not divide up what the others get; it draws its own current alongside them, and the supply has to carry the sum.
Every branch is across the same two points. A shared return conductor with resistance of its own breaks that, and the branches start affecting each other.
The connections have no resistance. In a real distribution board they do, which is why the far end of a busbar sits at a slightly lower voltage than the near end.
A ratio of two resistances — and what a load does to it

Two resistances in series carry one current, so the voltage at the point between them is the supply scaled by the lower resistance’s share of the pair. On paper it is a ratio, and the actual resistances do not matter — 1 kΩ and 1 kΩ divide by half, and so do 1 MΩ and 1 MΩ.

Connect something to that midpoint and the ratio stops being true. The load sits in parallel with the lower resistance, which lowers it, which moves the output down. How far depends entirely on the size of the divider against the load: a divider built from megohms collapses under almost any load, and one built from hundreds of ohms barely moves.

That trade-off is the whole design problem. Small resistances make a stiff output and waste current continuously; large ones waste almost nothing and cannot drive anything. It is why a divider is a fine way to make a reference voltage for something that draws no current, and a poor way to make a power supply.
The plain ratio assumes nothing is connected to the tap. Anything that draws current lowers the output, and this page shows by how much when you give it a load.
The supply holds its voltage. A battery with internal resistance sags under the divider’s own current before the division even starts.
This is a reference, not a power supply. Sizing a divider to feed a real load means burning far more current in the divider than the load draws.

How a current splits between two branches, and why the ratio looks backwards

Two branches across the same pair of nodes see the same voltage, so each carries a current set by its own resistance. The smaller resistance carries the larger share — which is obvious stated that way, and is exactly what the formula looks like it is saying the other way round.

The cross-over is the thing to hold onto: the current in the first branch is proportional to the *second* branch’s resistance. It is not a mistake in the formula. Raising the second branch’s resistance pushes more of the total down the first, so the first branch’s share genuinely does go up with the other branch’s value.

This is how a meter shunt works, and how a fault current divides between a protective conductor and any parallel metalwork that happens to be bonded alongside it.
Exactly two branches. With three, work out the parallel combination of the other two first and treat that as the second branch.
Resistances, not impedances. With reactance in a branch the split has a phase angle too, and the branch currents no longer add arithmetically.

Length, cross-section and temperature — where a cable\'s resistance actually comes from

A conductor's resistance is set by three things: how far the current has to travel, how much metal it has to travel through, and how hot that metal is. Length raises it in proportion; cross-section lowers it in proportion; temperature raises it by a few parts in a thousand per kelvin.

The material constant is resistivity — the resistance of a metre of the metal one square millimetre in section. Copper is about 0.0172 and aluminium about 0.0283, which is the whole reason an aluminium conductor has to be roughly one size larger than a copper one to do the same job.

The temperature correction is the part most often skipped, and it is not small. A copper conductor sitting at the 70 °C its PVC insulation is rated to is about a fifth more resistive than the same conductor at 20 °C. Size a cable on its cold resistance and you will under-report the voltage drop by that margin.
Direct current, or alternating current in a small conductor. Above about 50 mm² the skin effect pushes current toward the surface and the effective resistance rises.
The whole run is at one temperature. A cable that leaves a warm panel and crosses a cold roof space is not.
This is the resistance of one conductor. A circuit needs the current to come back, so voltage drop uses the loop — both conductors, which is the second figure here.
Charge does not pile up and energy does not appear — the two bookkeeping rules

The current law says that whatever arrives at a junction leaves it. Charge does not collect at a terminal, so the currents in and the currents out must balance exactly, at every instant.

The voltage law says that going once round a closed loop and back to where you started must bring you back to the same potential. So the drops around the loop add up to the sources driving it — no more, no less.

Between them these two rules solve every resistive network there is. The series and parallel formulas are not separate laws; they are what these two reduce to when the circuit is simple enough to see the answer without writing the equations out.
The circuit is lumped: components are points, and the wire between them is not part of the sum. At radio frequencies, or over a long enough run, that stops being true.
Signs are yours to keep straight. Pick a direction for each branch before you start; a current that comes out negative simply runs the other way.

Three numbers for one waveform, and which of them your meter is showing you

A sine spends most of its cycle below its peak, so quoting the peak would overstate what it can do. The RMS value is defined to fix that: it is the direct voltage that would heat the same resistance at the same rate. When a supply is called 230 V, that is the RMS figure, and the waveform actually reaches 325 V twice per cycle.

That peak is not a curiosity. Insulation, semiconductor ratings and clearances are all sized against it, which is why a component rated 250 V direct is not safe on a 230 V alternating supply.

The average of the rectified wave is a third figure, lower again, and it matters because cheap meters measure it and then scale it by 1.11 to display an RMS value. That scaling is only correct for a sine — on the distorted current a switch-mode supply draws, such a meter reads low, and a true-RMS instrument does not.
The waveform is a clean sine. Every factor here — 1.414, 1.11, 0.9 — is derived from that shape and none of them survives a distorted one.
A true-RMS meter measures the RMS value directly. An averaging meter infers it, and only a sine makes that inference right.
Why a capacitor passes more current the faster the supply alternates

A capacitor does not conduct. What flows is charge going in and out of it as the voltage rises and falls, and the faster that happens the more charge moves per second — which is to say, the larger the current.

Reactance is the ratio of voltage to current, so it falls as frequency rises and as capacitance rises. It is measured in ohms, but it is not resistance: no energy is converted to heat. The capacitor takes energy from the supply for a quarter of a cycle and hands all of it back for the next quarter.

That return is what makes a capacitor useful for power factor correction. The reactive current it draws is opposite in phase to what an inductive load draws, so the two can cancel and leave the supply carrying only the current that does work.
A sinusoidal supply at one frequency. On a distorted waveform each harmonic sees a different reactance, and the higher ones see much less of it.
The capacitor is ideal. A real one has series resistance and inductance in its leads, which matter well before radio frequencies for a large power capacitor.
The current leads the voltage by 90°. That phase shift is the whole point, and it is why this current does no work despite being real enough to melt a fuse.
Why a coil passes less current the faster the supply alternates

A coil resists a change in the current through it. Changing current changes the magnetic field, the changing field induces a voltage that opposes the change, and the faster the supply alternates the harder that opposition pushes back.

So reactance rises with frequency and with inductance, which is the opposite of a capacitor. Again the ohms are not resistance: energy goes into the magnetic field for a quarter cycle and comes back out for the next.

This is why almost every real load is inductive. Motors, transformers, contactor coils and discharge lighting all contain windings, and all of them draw a current that lags the voltage — which is the current a power factor correction capacitor is installed to cancel.
A sinusoidal supply at one frequency, as for a capacitor.
The coil is ideal. A real winding has resistance too, and for a contactor coil that resistance is a large part of what limits the current.
The core is not saturated. Once it is, inductance collapses and the current rises far beyond what this predicts — which is what an inrush current is.
Active, reactive and apparent power as three sides of one right triangle

When the current lags or leads the voltage, only part of what the supply carries does any work. Splitting the current into the part in phase with the voltage and the part at right angles to it splits the power the same way: active power, which does the work, and reactive power, which only moves back and forth.

Because the two components are at right angles they do not add arithmetically. They add as the sides of a right triangle, and the hypotenuse — apparent power — is what the cable and the transformer actually have to carry. That is why supply equipment is rated in kVA and not in kW.

The angle between the base and the hypotenuse is the phase angle, and its cosine is the power factor. Correcting the power factor means shortening the vertical side until the hypotenuse is nearly the base — the same work done with less current.
Voltage and current are both sinusoidal. With harmonics present there is a third kind of non-working power, and cos φ stops being the whole power factor.
This is displacement power factor — the phase shift only. A meter reporting true power factor on a distorted supply will read lower than this triangle suggests.

Where the √3 comes from, and which figure a nameplate is quoting

Three windings can be joined two ways. In star each winding runs between a line and a common point, so the voltage across a winding is the line voltage divided by √3 while the winding carries the full line current. In delta each winding runs between two lines, so it sees the full line voltage and carries the line current divided by √3.

The √3 is not a convention — it falls out of the geometry. Two phases 120° apart do not add head to tail; the vector sum of two equal phasors at 120° is √3 times one of them, and that is the whole derivation.

The practical consequence is that a motor wound for 400 V per winding runs in delta on a 400 V supply and in star on a 690 V one, and that starting a delta motor in star gives each winding 1/√3 of its rated voltage and therefore a third of its torque. Star-delta starting is exactly this arithmetic used on purpose.
The three phases are balanced. With unequal loading the neutral carries current and the phase voltages stop being equal.
Sinusoidal, no harmonics. Third harmonics add rather than cancel in the neutral, which is a separate problem this page does not model.
How long a capacitor takes to charge, and why it never quite finishes

Close a switch and the capacitor starts empty, so the whole supply appears across the resistor and the current is at its largest. As charge accumulates the capacitor voltage rises, the voltage left across the resistor falls, and the current falls with it. The charging slows down precisely because it has already got somewhere.

That self-limiting behaviour gives an exponential, and the time constant τ = R · C is its natural unit. After one τ the capacitor is 63 % of the way there, after three it is at 95 %, after five at 99.3 %. In principle it never arrives; in practice five time constants is called fully charged and nobody is misled.

The same curve runs backwards on discharge, which is why a large capacitor stays dangerous after isolation. A 1 mF capacitor bleeding through a 1 MΩ resistor has a time constant of a thousand seconds, so the five that count as discharged are nearly an hour and a half — with no indication on the outside that the time has not passed.
The supply is a step: it appears all at once and then holds. A ramp or an alternating supply gives a different curve entirely.
The capacitor is ideal and the source has no resistance of its own. A real source adds to R and lengthens τ.
It never reaches the supply voltage. Treat five time constants as charged, and never treat a capacitor as discharged because time has passed — measure it.

Why the two reactances subtract before anything is squared

An inductor makes the current lag the voltage and a capacitor makes it lead. The two effects are exactly opposite, so in a series circuit their reactances subtract: what the supply sees is the difference between them, not the sum.

That difference then combines with the resistance at right angles, because resistance and reactance are ninety degrees apart in phase. Squaring and adding under a root is the same right-triangle arithmetic as the power triangle, applied to ohms instead of watts.

The order matters and is the mistake to watch for. Subtract first, then square. A circuit with 100 Ω of inductive reactance and 100 Ω of capacitive reactance is purely resistive; adding them before squaring would report 141 Ω of reactance that is not there.
The three are in series, so one current passes through all of them. A parallel arrangement needs admittances and gives a different answer entirely.

The frequency where the reactances cancel, and how sharply they do it

Inductive reactance rises with frequency and capacitive reactance falls, so somewhere they are equal. At that frequency they cancel completely and the circuit is left with nothing but its resistance — the impedance is at its minimum and the current at its maximum.

How sharp that peak is depends on the resistance. The quality factor Q compares the reactance at resonance with the resistance; a low resistance gives a high Q and a narrow, tall peak, and a high resistance flattens it out. The bandwidth is the resonant frequency divided by Q.

Series resonance has a property that catches people out: at resonance the voltage across the inductor and across the capacitor can each be Q times the supply voltage. They are equal and opposite so they cancel at the terminals, but the insulation of each component sees the full magnified figure.
A series circuit. Parallel resonance peaks in impedance rather than dipping, and its formulas are not these.
The resistance is the whole loss. A real inductor\'s winding resistance and core loss both lower Q below what this reports.
Watch the component voltages. At high Q the inductor and the capacitor each carry many times the supply voltage, and rating them for the supply alone will destroy them.
Any linear network, seen from two terminals, is one source behind one resistance

However complicated a network of sources and resistances is, a load connected to two of its terminals cannot tell it apart from a single source in series with a single resistance. That is the whole theorem, and it is what makes a circuit with twenty components tractable.

The source voltage is what you measure across the terminals with nothing connected. The resistance is what you measure looking back into the terminals with every source replaced by its own internal resistance — an ideal voltage source becomes a short, an ideal current source becomes an open.

Once you have the pair, any load is a two-resistor problem. Change the load and you do not redo the network; you redo one division. That is why this is the theorem that makes load lines, matching and fault-level calculations possible at all.
The network is linear. A diode, a lamp filament or a saturating core breaks the superposition the proof rests on.
The equivalent is only equivalent at those two terminals. It says nothing about what happens inside, including how much power the original network dissipates.
Real sources are not ideal. A battery\'s own internal resistance belongs in R_th, and leaving it out is what makes a bench calculation disagree with a measurement.

The same network again, as a current source with the same resistance beside it

Norton says what Thévenin says, from the other side. Instead of a voltage source in series with a resistance, the network becomes a current source with that same resistance in parallel. The two forms are interchangeable and describe the same box.

The current is what would flow if you shorted the terminals, which is the Thévenin voltage divided by the Thévenin resistance. The resistance is unchanged. Converting between the two forms is one division in each direction.

Which form to reach for is a matter of what the rest of the circuit looks like. A load in series with the equivalent is easier with Thévenin; branches in parallel with it are easier with Norton, because parallel current sources add.
Same conditions as Thévenin: a linear network, equivalent only at the two terminals it was taken from.
The source resistance is never zero in practice. A Norton current source with no resistance beside it would deliver that current into anything, which nothing does.
The load that takes the most power — and why you almost never want it

A very small load takes a large current at a small voltage, and a very large load takes a large voltage at a small current. Both deliver little power. Somewhere between them is a maximum, and it falls exactly where the load resistance equals the source resistance.

At that point the load takes U²/4R, which is as much as the source can ever give it. But the source resistance is carrying the same current through the same resistance, so it is burning exactly as much — the efficiency at maximum power is one half.

That is why this theorem belongs to signal circuits and not to power systems. Matching an amplifier to a loudspeaker or an antenna to a feeder is worth doing because the signal is what matters and the wasted watt is negligible. Matching a distribution transformer to a building would mean losing as much in the transformer as the building used, which is why supply networks are built with the source resistance as low as it can be made instead.
This is a signal-circuit rule. In a power system the goal is efficiency, not maximum transfer, and the two point in opposite directions.
The source voltage and resistance are fixed and the load is what varies. If you can lower the source resistance instead, do that — it beats matching every time.
At the matched load the efficiency is one half. Read the efficiency figure below alongside the power one, always.
Turning three resistances inside out so a bridge network becomes solvable

Some networks cannot be reduced by series and parallel steps at all. A Wheatstone bridge is the standard example: no two of its five resistances are purely in series or purely in parallel, so the usual rules run out immediately.

The way through is to replace three of them with an equivalent set arranged the other way. A star of three resistances meeting at a hidden centre point, and a delta of three joining the same three terminals, can be made indistinguishable from outside. Swap one for the other and the network usually falls apart into series and parallel steps.

This is not the same thing as star and delta connection of a supply, despite the shared names. That one is about how windings are wired and where the √3 comes from; this one is a network reduction with no phases in it at all.
Equivalent at the three terminals only. The centre point of a star has no counterpart in the delta, so any voltage measured there is lost in the swap.
Resistances, not impedances. The same transformation works for impedances, but then every product and quotient is a complex one.
Not the same as star and delta supply connection. That topic is about windings and line voltages; this one is a network identity.
